summary: For ages 5–7, teach 'Dressing for the Weather' as a cause→choice routine: LOOK at today's weather first, THEN choose clothing/equipment that matches (rain→waterproofs; hot sun→hat, sunscreen, water, shade; cold→warm adjustable layers; wind→windproof). Each choice carries a short 'why' (a coat keeps rain off; layers trap body warmth; a hat and sunscreen protect skin), so children justify rather than only match. Centre a dress-a-character decision task where the child picks and then sees the comfort consequence, backed by matching/explanation checks and a real-outing performance task. Include sun safety as a genuine daily health habit, not just a beach activity.
misconceptions: 'Coats/jumpers make heat' — they TRAP your body's warmth (insulation), they don't generate heat; keep this simple but don't imply clothes are heaters.
'Sunscreen/hats are only for the beach' — sun protection matters on any strong-sun day, not just holidays.
'Dress for the season, not the day' — a cold summer day or mild winter day needs dressing for TODAY'S weather.
'More clothes are always warmer' — overheating is possible; layers you can adjust beat one huge coat.
'You only prepare for bad weather' — hot sunny weather also needs preparation (water, shade, sun cover).

activities.title: Dress the character, then see what happens
steps: Look at today's weather shown in a scene (ideally pull in the real local forecast so the decision matches the child's actual day).
Open a wardrobe of clothing/equipment (coat, umbrella, wellies, sun hat, sunscreen, water bottle, gloves, scarf, vest, jumper, t-shirt) and drag on what you think suits the weather.
Send the character outside and watch the outcome: in a t-shirt on a cool rainy day they come back dripping and shivering; with a raincoat and umbrella they splash about comfortably.
Switch to blazing sun: test good choices (sun hat, sunscreen, water bottle, t-shirt) versus a woolly jumper that leaves the character red and overheating.
Switch to a frosty morning: build up warm layers one at a time (vest → jumper → coat → gloves) and notice you can add or remove layers as conditions change.
For each round, say the little reason out loud ('the coat keeps the rain off', 'the hat shades my skin and eyes').
activities.insight: The clothing you choose follows from the weather you observe: look first, then choose, and each sensible choice has a reason tied to staying comfortable and safe.

activities.title: Get ready for real weather cards (performance task)
steps: Lay out a mix of real or pictured clothing and equipment: sun hat, sunscreen, warm coat, gloves, scarf, umbrella, wellies, t-shirt, water bottle.
Draw three weather cards: hot-and-sunny, cold-and-snowy, rainy.
For each card, get a doll (or yourself) ready to go outside by choosing the right items, and act it out (e.g. actually put the coat on for the cold card).
Say why each item suits that weather.
Link it to the day: 'How does this weather change what we can do at playtime or walking to school?'
activities.insight: A child who can assemble a sensible, condition-matched kit for several different conditions — and explain the choices — has connected weather observation to everyday preparation.

activities.title: Match weather to gear and say why
steps: Match each weather to its gear: rain → coat + umbrella; hot sun → sun hat + sunscreen; cold → hat + gloves + layers; wind → windproof.
For each match, answer a 'why do we wear this?' question in your own words.
Try a choice question such as 'What should you wear on a hot sunny day, and why not a woolly jumper?'
activities.insight: Children can pair conditions with appropriate gear and give a short reason for each pairing.

activities.title: Talk it through: why this, not that?
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'It's raining out — what should I wear, and why?'
Explain why the umbrella is needed on the rainy day, and why a sun hat and sunscreen are the main things to choose on the sunny day.
Say what could happen on a hot, sunny day if you went out with no hat and no sunscreen.
activities.insight: Putting the reasons into words strengthens the justification behind each clothing choice.

activities.title: Reference: dressed right for each weather
steps: Browse a scene of correctly-dressed figures for each weather, revealing a short 'why' under each (e.g. a flap you tap or lift).
Compare a dressed-right (comfortable) figure with a dressed-wrong (cold/wet/too hot) figure for the same weather.
activities.insight: Seeing a worked example of sensible clothing for each condition, with reasons, supports children who need a model before deciding themselves.

checkQuestion: Give the child a mix of clothing and equipment (sun hat, sunscreen, warm coat, gloves, scarf, umbrella, wellies, t-shirt) and three weather cards: hot-and-sunny, cold-and-snowy, rainy. Ask them to get a doll (or themselves) ready to go outside for each card, choosing the right items. Watch what they pick for each condition rather than asking them to explain the rule.
checkAnswer: Hot-and-sunny: sun hat, sunscreen, t-shirt (not a heavy coat). Cold-and-snowy: warm coat, gloves, scarf. Rainy: umbrella and wellies (waterproofs). The child assembles a sensible, condition-matched kit for each card and can act it out (e.g. actually puts the coat on for the cold card).
